title: Why do we find circles so beautiful?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The circle has been adopted in every imaginable domain of human experience, from money and art to architecture and religion. The interesting question is: why? The circle is everywhere in life and nature, but can this fact alone explain its central role in the cities we build, the objects we design, the visual symbols we create, and the numerous layers of cultural meaning we apply? A preference for circular shapes is deeply ingrained in all of us from birth. A 2011 eye-tracking study found that at five months of age, before they utter a word or scribble a drawing, infants already show a clear visual preference for curved lines over straight lines.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Over the last century, researchers on human perception have tried to explain our innate liking for circular and curvy shapes. In a 1921 study conducted by the Swedish psychologist Helge Lundholm, subjects were asked to draw lines representing a set of emotional adjectives. While angular lines were used to depict adjectives like hard, harsh and cruel, curved lines were the popular choice for adjectives like gentle, quiet and mild. Over the years, other studies trying to associate feelings with types of lines have confirmed Lundholm's findings.

Over the years, other studies trying to associate feelings with types of lines have confirmed Lundholm's findings.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In a seminal paper published in 2006 in Psychological Science, cognitive psychologists Moshe Bar and Maital Neta conducted an experiment in which 14 participants were shown 140 pairs of letters, patterns, and everyday objects, differing only in whether or not they were curved. The results were not completely surprising: participants showed a marked preference for curved items in all categories, particularly when it came to real objects. To better understand this bias, Bar and Neta conducted another study one year later, this time by mapping the same cognitive response using functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The results were quite conclusive. Sharp-cornered objects caused much greater activation of the amygdala region of the brain. The amygdala's primary function is to process stimuli that induce fear, anxiety, and aggressiveness and to deal with the resulting emotional reactions. In other words, angular shapes tend to trigger fear and therefore aversion and mistrust. Moreover, the authors of the study noted that 'the degree of amygdala activation was proportional to the degree of angularity or sharpness of the object presented, and inversely related to object preference.' There are, of course, obvious deviations from this response - such as certain chocolate bars, angular objects which people appreciate. As the authors point out, people's positive feelings towards these can override the usual effects of angularity and dominate their preference.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Most of the research in this area seems to point out an evidence that humans are naturally inclined to prefer shapes and objects that evoke safety and are not so fond of objects with sharp angles and pointed features, as they suggest threat and injury: think of the thorns and spines of a plant, the sharp teeth of an animal, or the cutting edge of a rock. This preference might still prove wise in an urban world lacking natural threats but abundant with man-made ones. As the ultimate opposite of the angular shape, the circle represents all of the attributes that attract us: it is a safe, gentle, pleasant, graceful, dreamy, and even beautiful shape that evokes calmness, peacefulness, and relaxation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A second evolutionary explanation for our round-shape liking is rooted in the idea that human faces and the emotions they express rely on simple geometric shapes. Just think of the number of expressions that emotions can represent using very basic configurations. In 1978, psychologist John Bassili conducted an experiment in which he applied one hundred luminescent dots to the faces of several actors, people he knew would show emotions clearly. These participants were then asked to make different expressions, such as 'happy', 'sad', 'surprised', and 'angry' and the results were videoed. In the final recording, with only the luminescent dots visible, the outcome was quite revealing: while expressions of anger showed acute downward V shapes (angled eyebrows, cheeks, and chin), expressions of happiness showed expansive, outward curved patterns (arched cheeks, eyes, and mouth). In other words, happy faces resembled an expansive circle, while angry faces resembled a downward triangle.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: From an evolutionary standpoint, the warm, positive emotions elicited by a circular shape could have their basis in our attraction to the roundness of an infant's face. The evolutionary advantages of these feelings for the continuation of the human species are obvious, particularly since previous studies have indicated an adult preference for infants with rounded features. This also explains a known cognitive predisposition called the 'baby-face bias'. This is a tendency to perceive adults with a prominent, high forehead or other neotenous facial features as being more naive, honest and innocent. The division between circular, happy faces versus triangular, angry faces seems to be rooted in two primordial human needs: to read our fellow humans' facial expressions and to detect a threat as quickly as possible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The third and last explanation for the universal appeal of the circle might be rooted in our own visual mechanisms and the way we view the world around us. The human eye is an organ so complex that half of our brain is dedicated to processing visual perception. The iris and pupil, responsible for filtering light into the retina, are themselves circular. Importantly, such spheres create a natural circular frame for our vision, which on its own could explain an innate preference for that geometric shape.

groups.title: Babies' faces and the human eye
content: From an evolutionary perspective, we need to feel attracted to the roundness of an infant's face. This might explain why we associate 'baby-faced' adults, who have features like a big, noticeable {{23}} , with certain child-like characteristics. Conversely, we tend to associate adults who have {{24}} faces with anger. This is partly due to another evolutionary necessity, because anger in other humans represents a {{25}} to us.

Another reason for the universal appeal of the circle lies in our eyes, which are extremely {{26}} . We see the world through a frame which is itself circular, thanks to the iris and pupils in our eyes.
